messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Editor
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Female Presence: Being alone with women, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun was a 26-year-old South Asian man who had come to treatment months after a police encounter that had left him feeling permanently changed. Before the event, he had been working as an editor, spending long hours at his desk at home and in a small shared office where he reviewed copy, answered messages, and kept to a steady routine with his wife. The incident occurred late one evening when he was stopped by police while returning home. What began as a routine questioning escalated into a frightening confrontation in close quarters, with officers positioned around him and one of them pressing into his space in a way that made escape feel impossible. Arjun later described becoming intensely aware of the physical details of the moment: the sharp temperature of the air against his skin, the feel of his body locked in an awkward position, and the smells in the environment that seemed to stay with him long after he was back home. In the days that followed, he found that when the memory returned, it did not come back as a simple story. It came with an overwhelming grief that surprised him, as though he were mourning something that had been taken from him in that moment and never returned.

In the weeks after the encounter, Arjun started to notice that even ordinary changes in temperature on his skin could pull him back into that night. Cold air from a fan, a sudden chill from stepping out of the shower, or the blast of an office air conditioner could make his body stiffen before he had time to think. He would feel a brief wave of strangeness, as if he were beginning to detach from the room around him and from his own body, and that unsettled him enough that he would stop what he was doing and try to ground himself by gripping the edge of a table or pressing his feet into the floor. He also became uneasy about being alone with women, something he had not previously worried about. At home and at work, if he found himself in a room alone with a female colleague or a client’s wife dropping by to discuss text changes, he became watchful and tense, wanting the interaction to end quickly. He could not easily explain this to anyone, and the awkwardness of it made him withdraw further from situations that once had felt normal and unremarkable.

The memory of the police encounter remained vivid in a way that felt invasive rather than deliberate. At times, when the scene came to mind, Arjun would suddenly catch a smell that seemed to belong to that night, and the sensation would be so immediate that he would pause mid-sentence, trying to orient himself back to the present. He described these moments as though his body remembered before his mind did. There were times when the recollection brought a bodily reenactment as well, so that he felt himself back in the same position he had been forced into during the event, shoulders tense and body fixed, as if he were once again unable to move freely. These experiences were especially difficult when he was working, because editing required concentration and sustained attention, and he found that a line of text or a passing thought could open the door to a sudden, unwanted return of the event. Over time he began avoiding the office when he could and preferred to work from home, where he could control the environment more carefully.

As the months passed, Arjun increasingly judged himself harshly for how he had been coping. He spoke with embarrassment about how his own reactions had made him feel like a lousy coper, someone who should have been able to “handle it” better but had instead become more limited, more cautious, and more dependent on routines that felt fragile. He had once taken pride in being reliable and composed, but now he saw his reactions as evidence that he was failing himself and perhaps failing his wife as well. That sense of failure sat alongside a broader loss of meaning that he could not shake. The work he had once found intellectually satisfying now felt flat, and even at home he struggled to feel that his days were adding up to anything worthwhile. He would go through the motions of meals, work tasks, and conversation, but inside he felt that nothing in his life carried the same significance it had before.

By the time he sought help, Arjun was no longer trying to pretend that the problem was passing. He had become tired of measuring each day by what might set off the memory, whether a cold draft on his arms, an unexpectedly close interaction with a woman, or the first subtle sense that the world was slipping away from him. He came to treatment because he was afraid that nothing good could happen to him anymore, that the future had narrowed into a series of cautious days with little room for ease or hope. At the same time, he was quietly hoping that the intensity of grief, the intrusive sensory returns, and the self-judgment that had taken hold of him might begin to loosen, so that he could feel present again in his work, in his marriage, and in his own life.
